extracted.subtask_description: A collection of theorems, definitions, and technical hypotheses used in Lebesgue integration on Euclidean space: change-of-variables (polar/spherical), gamma function, Sard's theorem and lower-dimensional sets, Hardy–Littlewood maximal theorem and covering lemma, convolution/approximate identities and Fourier-series results, and Stieltjes measures on R.

rubrics_metrics.name: Polar change-of-variables for Lebesgue integral (R^2)
rubrics_metrics.description:
For every nonnegative Borel function f on R^2, one can change to polar coordinates and write
∬_{R^2} f(x,y) dx dy = ∫_{0}^{∞} ∫_{0}^{2π} f(r cos θ, r sin θ) r dθ dr, 
with the usual harmless exceptional set on the x-axis having Lebesgue measure 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The formula holds as stated for nonnegative Borel f; the omission of the part of the x-axis with x<0 (or another negligible exceptional set coming from the coordinate map) is harmless because that set has measure 0. This is the prototypical application of the change-of-variables formula together with Fubini's theorem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spherical coordinates change-of-variables in R^N
rubrics_metrics.description:
Using the N-dimensional spherical-coordinate map ϕ(r, θ1,...,θ_{N-1}) = r·ω(θ), integration over R^N can be written
∫_{R^N} f(x) dx = ∫_{0}^{∞} ∫_{S^{N-1}} f(r ω) r^{N-1} dω dr = ∫_{0}^{∞} ∫_{θ} f(r cos θ1, ...) r^{N-1} (sin^{N-2}θ1 sin^{N-3}θ2···) dθ dr
for appropriate parameter ranges, interpreting dω as the rotation-invariant measure on S^{N-1}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Problem 2 at the chapter end lists the checks needed: (i) the Jacobian determinant (the 'determinant factor') equals the stated r^{N-1}·(product of sines) factor; (ii) ϕ is one-to-one on its domain U; (iii) the complement of ϕ(U) in R^N is a lower-dimensional set. If these hold, the change-of-variables formula applies and integration over ϕ(U) can be extended over all R^N.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exceptional/ lower-dimensional sets have measure zero (definition + corollary)
rubrics_metrics.description: A lower-dimensional set in R^N is any set contained in a countable union of smooth images of open sets in Euclidean spaces of dimension < N. Any such lower-dimensional set is Lebesgue measurable and has Lebesgue measure 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This formalizes the intuition that images of lower-dimensional manifolds (or countable unions thereof) are negligible for N-dimensional Lebesgue measure; it is used to justify extending integration domains in change-of-variables arguments when the coordinate map omits a lower-dimensional subset.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of critical point/value and Sard's Theorem
rubrics_metrics.description: If ϕ: V → R^N (V open in R^N) is smooth, a critical point x is one where Dϕ(x) has rank < N; a critical value is ϕ(x) for a critical point x. Sard's Theorem: the set of critical values of a smooth map ϕ:V→R^N is a Borel set of Lebesgue measure 0 in R^N.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof outline: cover V by compact geometric rectangles, approximate ϕ locally by its first-order linearization L_x, use bounds on the remainder to show images of small neighborhoods lie in small-volume boxes, subdivide and let mesh → 0 to conclude outer measure arbitrarily small. Consequence: images of maps from lower-dimensional domains are negligible in R^N.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gamma function definition and integrability condition
rubrics_metrics.description: For s with Re s > 0 define Γ(s) = ∫_{0}^{∞} t^{s-1} e^{-t} dt. The integrand t^{s-1} e^{-t} is continuous (hence Borel measurable) on (0,∞), and integrable for Re s > 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To check integrability, one may treat integrability near 0 and near ∞ separately; use comparisons (e.g., t^{Re s -1} near 0, and exponential decay near ∞) and possibly bound via elementary inequalities. The definition extends Γ to complex s with Re s > 0.

rubrics_metrics.name: Basic identities and special values of Γ (Proposition 6.34)
rubrics_metrics.description: The gamma function satisfies: (a) Γ(s+1) = s Γ(s) for Re s > 0; (b) Γ(1) = 1; (c) Γ(1/2) = √π and Γ(n+1) = n! for integers n > 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Part (a) follows by integration by parts on [ε, M] and passage to limits as ε→0, M→∞. Part (c) can be obtained by suitable change of variables and evaluating Gaussian integrals (use Proposition 6.33 for ∫ e^{-π x^2} dx = 1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Hardy–Littlewood maximal function and its weak (1,1) bound (Theorem 6.38)
rubrics_metrics.description:
For f ∈ L^1(R^N) define the Hardy–Littlewood maximal function
f^*(x) = sup_{r>0} (1/m(rB)) ∫_{rB} |f(x-y)| dy (equivalently average of |f| over translates of dilates of a fixed neighborhood B).
Then for every ξ > 0, m({x : f^*(x) > ξ}) ≤ C_N · ||f||_1 / ξ where the text gives C_N = 5^N (i.e., the operator maps L^1 to weak-L^1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequences: f^* is finite almost everywhere; the inequality is quantitative and is proved using a geometric covering lemma (Wiener's Covering Lemma) together with disjointness and additivity estimates. This weak-type (1,1) bound is the key to many a.e. convergence results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and properties of the maximal function (measurability, non-integrability)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Hardy–Littlewood maximal function f^* is measurable (sup over rational radii gives same value) and is not generally in L^1 unless f ≡ 0, but is 'close' to integrable in the sense given by Theorem 6.38 (weak L^1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One shows measurability via supremum over countable set; f^* typically behaves like a multiple of 1/|x|^N at infinity for compactly supported f, hence fails to be integrable, but its level set decay ∼ 1/ξ makes it weak-L^1.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiation theorem via maximal inequality (Corollary 6.39)
rubrics_metrics.description:
If f is integrable on every bounded subset of R^N, then for a.e. x,
lim_{r→0} (1/m(rB)) ∫_{rB} f(x-y) dy = f(x).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses approximation of f by a compactly supported continuous g and the maximal inequality for the difference; the maximal operator controls limsup deviations and yields almost-everywhere differentiation of averages (Lebesgue differentiation theorem for this averaging family).

rubrics_metrics.name: Wiener's Covering Lemma (geometric covering tool, Lemma 6.41)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let E ⊆ R^N be Borel and suppose to each x∈E is associated a ball B(r(x); x) with radii bounded. Then there exists a finite or countable disjoint subcollection {B(r_j; x_j)} such that E ⊆ ⋃_j B(5 r_j; x_j) and m(E) ≤ 5^N ∑_j m(B(r_j; x_j)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The lemma is proved by greedy selection of balls of near-maximal radius and throwing away those that intersect already-chosen balls, producing disjointness and the required covering with a fixed dilation factor (5 here). This is the core geometric ingredient in the maximal theorem proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maximal control of convolution with radial decreasing kernels (Corollary 6.42)
rubrics_metrics.description:
Let ϕ(x) = ϕ_0(|x|) where ϕ_0 is a decreasing C^1 function on [0,∞) with ∫_{R^N} ϕ = 1. Define ϕ_ε(x) = ε^{-N} ϕ(x/ε). Then there exists C_ϕ such that for all f∈L^1(R^N) and all x,
sup_{ε>0} |(ϕ_ε * f)(x)| ≤ C_ϕ f^*(x). Consequently (ϕ_ε * f)(x) → f(x) a.e. for f∈L^1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses radial monotonicity to compare ϕ_ε averages with averages over balls and then Theorem 6.38 to obtain weak-(1,1) control. Typical examples are Poisson kernels; this yields boundary convergence results and approximate-identity convergence a.e.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fejér kernels as approximate identities and convergence results (Theorem 6.48)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Fejér kernel K_N on the circle is a trigonometric polynomial with properties: (i) K_N ≥ 0; (ii) (1/2π) ∫_{-π}^{π} K_N(x) dx = 1; (iii) for any δ>0, sup_{|x|≥δ} K_N(x) → 0 as N→∞. Consequently K_N * f → f in L^1 for f∈L^1, in L^2 if f∈L^2, pointwise at continuity points and uniformly on compact sets where f is continuous/uniformly continuous; also at jump discontinuities the Cesàro sums converge to the average of the one-sided limits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fejér's kernel is the canonical approximate identity for periodic functions; the three properties above are the axioms that yield convolution convergence in various norms and pointwise settings, and they allow proofs of Parseval, uniqueness, and summability results for Fourier series in the Lebesgue setting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parseval's Theorem for L^2 (Theorem 6.49)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f∈L^2 on [-π,π] with Fourier coefficients {c_n}, then (1/2π) ∫_{-π}^{π} |f(x)|^2 dx = ∑_{n=-∞}^{∞} |c_n|^2, and the partial Fourier sums s_N(f) converge to f in L^2 (i.e., ||f - s_N(f)||_2 → 0).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses the minimization property of Fourier partial sums (orthogonal projection in L^2), Bessel's inequality, and the Fejér kernel to pass to limits. Parseval identifies L^2-norm with ℓ^2 norm of Fourier coefficients.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniqueness of Fourier coefficients in L^1 (Corollary 6.50)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f∈L^1 has all Fourier coefficients equal to 0 then f is the zero element of L^1 (i.e., f = 0 a.e.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses convolution with Fejér kernels K_N: K_N * f are continuous with zero Fourier coefficients so K_N * f ≡ 0; since K_N * f → f in L^1, f ≡ 0.

rubrics_metrics.name: Riesz–Fischer theorem (existence in L^2 from ℓ^2 sequences, Theorem 6.51)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a doubly-infinite sequence {c_n} with ∑_{n=-∞}^{∞} |c_n|^2 < ∞, there exists f∈L^2 whose Fourier coefficients are exactly {c_n} and whose Fourier series ∑ c_n e^{inx} converges to f in L^2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct partial sums f_N(x) = ∑_{|n|≤N} c_n e^{inx}; the Parseval identity implies {f_N} is Cauchy in L^2, hence converges (completeness of L^2) to f; continuity of the inner product gives the coefficient identities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stieltjes measures on R and distribution functions (definition and correspondence, Theorem 6.52)
rubrics_metrics.description: A Stieltjes measure µ is a Borel measure on R. Its distribution function F(x) is defined by F(x) = µ((0,x]) if x>0, F(0)=0, and F(x) = -µ((x,0]) if x<0. The function F satisfies: (i) F is nondecreasing; (ii) F is right-continuous; (iii) F(0)=0. Conversely, any function F with these properties determines a unique Stieltjes measure µ via µ((a,b]) = F(b) - F(a) (and corresponding limits for other interval types).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct µ initially on bounded intervals via differences of F and extend additively to finite disjoint unions of bounded intervals (elementary sets), then extend to Borel σ-algebra. This gives the one-to-one correspondence between monotone right-continuous functions and Borel measures on R (Stieltjes measures).

rubrics_metrics.name: Stieltjes measure properties and construction details
rubrics_metrics.description: Given F with (i)-(iii), define µ((a,b]) = F(b)-F(a) and extend to µ on the ring of finite disjoint unions of bounded intervals by additivity. The distribution function F uniquely determines the measure µ and µ((a,b]) = F(b) - F(a).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Right-continuity and monotonicity of F ensure that the set function is well-defined and countably additive on increasing unions. The construction mirrors Lebesgue's treatment of measure from an outer measure on intervals.
